title: Indian Economy (1950–1990)
description: Class 12 Economics: India's economic planning and Five-Year Plans, the goals of planning, land reforms and the Green Revolution, and the industrial policy, public sector and import substitution.

topics.title: Economic Planning and the Five-Year Plans
topics.concept:
After independence, India chose the path of economic planning to develop its weak economy. India became a mixed economy — combining a large public sector with a private sector. The Planning Commission was set up in 1950 (with the Prime Minister as chairman) to prepare Five-Year Plans — plans setting targets for the economy over five-year periods. (In 2015 the Planning Commission was replaced by NITI Aayog.)

The plans pursued four long-term goals of planning:

  • Growth — increasing the country's output (GDP) and capacity to produce.
  • Modernisation — adopting new technology and changing social outlook (e.g. equal rights for women).
  • Self-reliance — avoiding dependence on imports and foreign aid by producing things at home.
  • Equity — ensuring the benefits of growth reach all, reducing inequality and poverty.

The early plans shaped India's strategy. The First Five-Year Plan (1951–56), based on the Harrod–Domar model, gave top priority to agriculture and irrigation (e.g. the Bhakra-Nangal dam), to recover from the food shortages of partition. The Second Five-Year Plan (1956–61), based on the Mahalanobis model, shifted the focus to heavy industry (steel plants, machine-making) in the public sector, believing that building basic industries was the key to long-term growth. These two priorities — agriculture and heavy industry — defined India's planned development for decades.

examples.problem: Example 1: When was the Planning Commission set up, and what was its job?
examples.solution:
It prepared the plans.

  • Set up in 1950.
  • To prepare India's Five-Year Plans (replaced by NITI Aayog in 2015).
examples.answer: The Planning Commission was set up in 1950 to prepare India's Five-Year Plans (it was replaced by NITI Aayog in 2015).

examples.problem: Example 2: Name the four goals of economic planning in India.
examples.solution:
Recall the four.

  • Growth, modernisation, self-reliance and equity.

examples.problem: Example 3: What was the priority of the First and Second Five-Year Plans?
examples.solution:
Agriculture then heavy industry.

  • First Plan (1951–56): agriculture.
  • Second Plan (1956–61): heavy industry (Mahalanobis model).
examples.answer: The First Plan focused on agriculture; the Second Plan focused on heavy industry (the Mahalanobis model).

recap:
• India chose planning & a mixed economy; Planning Commission (1950) made Five-Year Plans (→ NITI Aayog in 2015).
  • Four goals: growth, modernisation, self-reliance, equity.
  • First Plan (1951–56): agriculture (Harrod–Domar); Second Plan (1956–61): heavy industry (Mahalanobis).

quiz.q: The Planning Commission was set up in:
quiz.explanation: The Planning Commission was established in 1950.

quiz.q: Which is a goal of Indian economic planning?
quiz.explanation: Self-reliance (with growth, modernisation, equity) is a goal of planning.

topics.title: Agriculture: Land Reforms and the Green Revolution
topics.concept:
Since most Indians depended on farming, agriculture was central to planning. Two big efforts were made to transform it: land reforms and the Green Revolution.

Land reforms aimed to make landholding fairer and farming more productive. They included:

  • Abolition of intermediaries (zamindari abolition) — ending the exploitative zamindar class so that the actual tiller could own the land. This was the most successful reform.
  • Tenancy reforms — giving tenants security and fair rents.
  • Land ceiling — fixing a maximum amount of land a person could own, so surplus land could be given to the landless. (This was poorly implemented in many states.)
  • Consolidation of holdings — combining scattered small plots into one, to farm more efficiently.

The biggest breakthrough was the Green Revolution of the mid-1960s. It was the use of High-Yielding Variety (HYV) seeds, along with more fertilisers, irrigation and modern methods, which dramatically raised the output of wheat and rice. Its results were historic: India moved from food shortages and dependence on imports to self-sufficiency in food grains, and the government could build a buffer stock for food security. However, the Green Revolution had limits — its benefits were concentrated in a few regions (Punjab, Haryana, western UP) and mainly helped larger farmers, increasing some inequalities. Still, achieving food self-sufficiency was one of independent India's greatest successes.

examples.problem: Example 1: Name any two land reforms in India.
examples.solution:
Aimed at fairer, productive farming.

  • Abolition of intermediaries (zamindari abolition) and land ceiling.
  • (Also tenancy reforms and consolidation of holdings.)
examples.answer: Abolition of intermediaries (zamindari abolition) and land ceiling (also tenancy reforms and consolidation of holdings).

examples.solution:
HYV seeds and modern inputs.

  • The use of high-yielding variety (HYV) seeds, with more fertilisers and irrigation.
  • It greatly raised the output of wheat and rice (from the mid-1960s).
examples.answer: The Green Revolution was the use of HYV seeds with more fertilisers and irrigation from the mid-1960s, which greatly raised wheat and rice output.

examples.problem: Example 3: What was the most important result of the Green Revolution?
examples.solution:
India fed itself.

  • India became self-sufficient in food grains and built a buffer stock.
examples.answer: India became self-sufficient in food grains (and could build a buffer stock), ending dependence on food imports.

recap:
• Land reforms: abolition of intermediaries (zamindari abolition — most successful), tenancy reforms, land ceiling, consolidation of holdings.
  • Green Revolution (mid-1960s): HYV seeds + fertilisers + irrigation → big rise in wheat & rice → food self-sufficiency + buffer stock.
  • Limits: concentrated in a few regions (Punjab, Haryana, W-UP) and helped larger farmers more.

quiz.q: The most successful land reform was the:
quiz.explanation: Abolition of intermediaries was the most successful land reform.

quiz.q: The Green Revolution made India self-sufficient in:
quiz.explanation: It brought self-sufficiency in food grains (wheat and rice).

topics.title: Industry: Policy, Public Sector and Import Substitution
topics.concept:
Industrial development was the other pillar of planning. The framework was set by the Industrial Policy Resolution of 1956 (IPR 1956), which classified industries into three categories: those exclusively for the public sector (defence, heavy industry), those where the public sector would lead but private firms could join, and those left to the private sector (under licensing). The public sector was given the "commanding heights" of the economy.

The public sector (government-owned firms) was thus made the leader of industrialisation. The reasons: private firms lacked the capital for huge basic industries (steel, power, machinery), and the government wanted to reduce inequality, develop backward regions and keep key industries in public hands. Large public-sector units like the steel plants (Bhilai, Rourkela, Durgapur) were built in this period.

India also followed a strategy of import substitution — producing goods at home instead of importing them, to become self-reliant. Domestic industry was protected from foreign competition through high tariffs (taxes on imports) and quotas (limits on imports). Industries also needed a government licence to start, expand or change production (the "licence raj").

This strategy had successes — India built a broad industrial base and reduced dependence on imports. But it also had serious drawbacks: protected from competition, many industries became inefficient and produced poor-quality, high-cost goods; the licence system caused delays, red tape and corruption; and the economy grew slowly (the so-called "Hindu rate of growth" of about 3.5% a year). By 1990 these problems, along with a financial crisis, set the stage for the major economic reforms of 1991 — the subject of the next chapter.

examples.problem: Example 1: What did the Industrial Policy Resolution of 1956 do?
examples.solution:
It classified industries and gave the public sector the lead.

  • It put industries into three categories.
  • It gave the public sector the 'commanding heights' of the economy.
examples.answer: The IPR 1956 classified industries into three categories and gave the public sector the 'commanding heights' of the economy.

examples.problem: Example 2: What is meant by import substitution?
examples.solution:
Make at home, not import.

  • Producing goods at home instead of importing them, to become self-reliant.
  • Domestic industry was protected by tariffs and quotas.
examples.answer: Import substitution means producing goods domestically instead of importing them (protected by tariffs and quotas) to become self-reliant.

examples.problem: Example 3: State one drawback of the protected, licence-based industrial strategy.
examples.solution:
Protection bred inefficiency.

  • Protected from competition, many industries became inefficient, producing high-cost, poor-quality goods.
  • (Also red tape/corruption from the licence raj.)
examples.answer: Many protected industries became inefficient, producing high-cost, poor-quality goods (and the licence raj caused delays and corruption).

recap:
• IPR 1956: three categories of industries; public sector given the commanding heights (steel plants — Bhilai, Rourkela, Durgapur).
  • Import substitution: produce at home, protect industry with tariffs/quotas; start/expand needs a licence (licence raj).
  • Successes (industrial base, less import dependence) but drawbacks: inefficiency, poor quality, red tape, slow growth ("Hindu rate" ~3.5%) → led to 1991 reforms.

quiz.q: The 'commanding heights' of the economy were given to the:
quiz.explanation: IPR 1956 gave the public sector the commanding heights.

quiz.q: Producing goods at home instead of importing them is:
quiz.explanation: Import substitution replaces imports with home production.

questions.q: After independence, India became a:
questions.explanation: India chose a mixed economy.

questions.q: The Planning Commission was set up in:
questions.explanation: The Planning Commission was set up in 1950.

questions.q: In 2015 the Planning Commission was replaced by:
questions.explanation: NITI Aayog replaced the Planning Commission in 2015.

questions.q: Which is NOT a goal of Indian planning?
questions.explanation: The goals are growth, modernisation, self-reliance and equity.

questions.q: The First Five-Year Plan (1951–56) focused on:
questions.explanation: The First Plan prioritised agriculture.

questions.q: The Second Five-Year Plan (1956–61) focused on:
questions.explanation: The Second Plan focused on heavy industry.

questions.q: Ending the zamindar class so the tiller could own land is:
questions.explanation: Abolition of intermediaries (zamindari abolition).

questions.q: Fixing a maximum amount of land a person can own is the:
questions.explanation: A land ceiling sets the maximum holding.

questions.q: The Green Revolution used:
questions.explanation: It used HYV seeds with fertilisers and irrigation.

questions.q: The Green Revolution mainly raised the output of:
questions.explanation: It raised wheat and rice output.

questions.q: The Green Revolution made India self-sufficient in:
questions.explanation: It achieved food-grain self-sufficiency.

questions.q: The Industrial Policy Resolution of 1956 gave the lead to the:
questions.explanation: IPR 1956 gave the public sector the commanding heights.

questions.q: Producing goods at home instead of importing them is:
questions.explanation: That strategy is import substitution.

questions.q: The system requiring a government permit to start or expand industry was the:
questions.explanation: The licensing system was called the licence raj.

questions.q: A major drawback of protecting industry from competition was:
questions.explanation: Protection bred inefficiency and poor quality.

questions.q: The Second Plan's focus on heavy industry reflected the belief that building basic industries (steel, machines) would:
options: Lay the foundation for long-term, self-reliant growth
questions.explanation: Heavy industry was seen as the base that would enable the economy to make its own capital goods and grow.

questions.q: The Green Revolution is praised for food self-sufficiency but criticised because its gains were:
options: Concentrated in a few regions and among larger farmers
questions.explanation: Punjab, Haryana and western UP and bigger farmers benefited most, widening some regional and class inequalities.

questions.q: Why did the government build a buffer stock of food grains after the Green Revolution?
options: For food security and to stabilise prices
questions.explanation: Surplus grain was stored to ensure supply in bad years and to steady food prices through the PDS.

questions.q: Import substitution made many Indian industries inefficient mainly because protection removed the pressure of:
questions.explanation: Shielded from rivals, firms had little incentive to cut costs or improve quality.

questions.q: Land-ceiling laws often failed in practice because they were:
questions.explanation: Weak enforcement and loopholes (e.g. transfers to relatives) limited the redistribution of surplus land.

questions.q: The public sector was given the lead in heavy industry partly because private firms:
options: Lacked the huge capital needed for basic industries
questions.explanation: Massive, long-gestation projects like steel needed state capital that private investors could not raise.

questions.q: The slow growth of this era (about 3.5% a year) is sometimes nicknamed the:
questions.explanation: The persistently modest ~3.5% growth came to be called the 'Hindu rate of growth'.

questions.q: Abolition of intermediaries succeeded more than other land reforms because it:
options: Directly removed the exploitative zamindar layer
questions.explanation: Removing intermediaries gave many cultivators direct ownership, a clear and largely achievable goal.

questions.q: The combination of public-sector leadership, import substitution and licensing is described as an ____ growth strategy.
questions.explanation: Focusing on the home market behind protection, rather than world trade, made it an inward-looking strategy.

questions.q: By 1990, the problems of inefficiency, red tape and slow growth, plus a crisis, set the stage for the:
questions.explanation: These accumulated weaknesses, with a 1991 balance-of-payments crisis, triggered the LPG reforms of 1991.
